claims.statement: Current employer descriptions place Forward Deployed Engineers across discovery, implementation, deployment, adoption, and field feedback rather than at software delivery alone.
Current deployment-oriented employer materials explicitly connect technical delivery to measurable customer workflow results.
A service is understood through the outcome it enables across the user's path, not solely through a digital interface.
Outcome leadership does not remove the need for explicit access, policy, approval, privacy, and risk-ownership boundaries.
The deployed-outcome lifecycle in this book is an original synthesis and operating model rather than a formal external standard.
Evidence of software release or user activity is not by itself complete evidence of sustained workflow value inside guardrails.
Forward Deployed Software Engineer is used here as a narrower engineering-heavy employer title rather than as a universal synonym for every FDE role.
Some current FDE descriptions explicitly include codifying field patterns, tools, playbooks, reusable building blocks, and product feedback.
Discovery should begin with the user's whole problem and context rather than a preselected technical solution.
Interviews, observation, and existing evidence provide distinct inputs for learning how real users perform a workflow.
Access and data collection should be tied to a named discovery question and limited by purpose, owner, handling, and expiry.
Stakeholder opinion is evidence of what a person reports and should remain an assumption about the workflow until it is tested appropriately.
End-to-end and front-to-back discovery includes channels, operational processes, technology, and security rather than the visible interface alone.
The stakeholder and evidence models in this chapter are original synthesis tools for separating impact, knowledge, access, responsibility, authority, and confidence.
A current-state workflow model should cover the user's whole journey and broken handoffs rather than only the proposed interface.
Observation of real users can expose differences between reported procedure, actual work, and solution-shaped requirements.
Journey and experience maps can expose cross-channel handoffs and gaps that are invisible in a single service component.
BPMN 2.0.2 is a standardized process notation, but its existence does not make it mandatory or sufficient for workflow discovery.
Technical retry behavior can change the operational workflow because method semantics, caller intent, and ambiguous completion determine the next decision.
The coordinated workflow views and resolution test in this chapter are an original synthesis for deployment decisions rather than a formal modeling standard.
Outcome and use measures should be defined early enough to guide service decisions rather than added only after launch.
Benefits require an explicit baseline and continuing evidence that can support continue, change, or stop decisions.
Use, satisfaction, dropout, and segmented workflow evidence are complementary signals and should not be treated as interchangeable proof of value.
User-relevant service indicators and objectives are useful when they are connected to explicit actions and tradeoffs.

A vendor customer story reports 98 percent active use by Morgan Stanley advisor teams, but the figure remains attributed and does not independently prove productivity, correctness, or customer benefit.
An outcome contract should make it possible to continue, change, reduce, or stop a deployment when benefit and guardrail evidence do not justify the path.
The metric-tree, attribution-ladder, and outcome-contract structures in this chapter are original synthesis tools rather than formal external standards.
Current deployment-oriented employer materials describe diagnosing and prioritizing workflows before building or deploying the path.
Architecture and scope decisions involve explicit tradeoffs across reliability, security, operational excellence, performance, cost, and other contextual quality concerns.
Benefits evidence should allow a team to continue, change, reduce, or stop the planned path rather than treating completion as predetermined.
A smaller feature list is not necessarily a safer production path when it omits representative security, reliability, operating, or ownership constraints.
The scope-cone, must-prove/must-build/defer/reject, and uncertainty-to-experiment structures in this chapter are original synthesis tools rather than formal external standards.
Production exposure should not be used merely to discover whether an unacceptable safety, privacy, or authorization control works.
The C4 model provides hierarchical context and container abstractions without requiring one notation or diagramming tool.
Architecture decisions should make operational, security, reliability, performance, cost, identity, and failure tradeoffs explicit rather than maximize one attribute in isolation.
Network location alone is not a sufficient basis for trust; resource access requires explicit authentication and authorization appropriate to the request.
A first-party Cloudflare postmortem distinguishes configured state from operational state and reports recovery complexity across divergent distributed states.
A first-party Cloudflare postmortem reports that control-plane and data-plane separation limited one class of impact while the impaired control plane remained operationally consequential.
A structural diagram does not by itself establish runtime ownership, trust, data authority, failure propagation, or recovery behavior.
The responsibility, trust, data, runtime, and failure annotations in this chapter are an original extension used for FDE deployment decisions rather than a formal C4 standard.
OpenAPI 3.2.0 and AsyncAPI 3.0.0 provide versioned machine-readable descriptions for HTTP and message-driven interfaces respectively.
JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 can express structural validation but cannot by itself establish business meaning or workflow correctness.
HTTP method idempotency semantics do not alone establish application-level retry safety or preserve caller intent.
Client request identifiers can support safe retry only when the service defines semantic equivalence, conflicts, retention, completion, and late-arrival behavior.
ISO/IEC 25012 defines a general structured-data quality model that can inform contextual requirements and evaluation without prescribing local thresholds.
Semantic Versioning communicates compatibility expectations only after a public API is declared and does not replace deployment, schema, or data migration design.
An interface description or schema does not by itself establish ownership, ordering, consistency, timeout, retry, error, observability, support, or reconciliation behavior.
Exactly-once business effects are not obtained merely by applying an exactly-once label to message delivery or processing.
The interface catalog, semantic data contract, and reconciliation structures in this chapter are original FDE synthesis tools rather than formal standards.
Customer-environment architecture requires contextual tradeoffs across reliability, security, performance, operations, cost, and capacity rather than a provider-neutral claim of perfect parity.
Trust should be evaluated for each resource request and should not be inherited solely from network location.
Deployments that use OAuth 2.0 should account for RFC 9700 security best current practice within their actual flow and threat context.
Environment parity is often incomplete, so consequential differences require explicit tests, controls, monitoring, or accepted gaps.
A first-party Cloudflare postmortem reports that an access dependency complicated rollback and discusses break-glass access and tested known-good recovery identifiers.
Private networking, IP allowlisting, or placement inside a VPC does not by itself establish user or workload identity, least privilege, tenant isolation, or data-residency compliance.
The environment-difference matrix and topology/identity/configuration records in this chapter are original FDE synthesis tools rather than formal external standards.
AI risk management should be lifecycle- and use-case-specific and the cited framework version/revision state should remain visible.
A simpler deterministic or composable workflow is preferable when it satisfies the operational requirement without unnecessary autonomy or uncertainty.
Evaluation design benefits from explicit task, trial, data, grader, transcript or outcome, harness, suite, and capability-versus-regression distinctions.
Agentic behavior requires bounded tools and data plus ground truth, checkpoints, stopping conditions, and recovery appropriate to consequence.
The model is one component inside a broader production system that includes data, interfaces, controls, evaluation, monitoring, operation, and users.
Deployment-like simulation can expose behavior missed by static evaluation while still leaving production-tail limitations.
Human review does not automatically make an AI-assisted workflow safe, attentive, scalable, qualified, or accountable.
Current generative-AI risk and security taxonomies can prompt system-specific discovery but do not provide complete threat coverage or certification.
The NIST AI RMF 1.0 was under active revision at the research cutoff and should be cited as a versioned framework rather than timeless current status.

The specific OpenAI Evals platform documented at the research cutoff was scheduled for late-2026 deprecation, so durable prose should teach portable evaluation concepts rather than interface promises.
Network location alone does not establish trust; authorization decisions should protect named resources in the context of each request.
OAuth 2.0 deployments should apply RFC 9700 within their actual flow and threat model rather than treating protocol use as a security claim.
A versioned cybersecurity framework can organize desired outcomes and governance conversations but does not prescribe, verify, or certify a complete implementation.
Secure software practices should be integrated across the development lifecycle rather than deferred to one final security gate.
A privacy risk framework supports contextual organizational risk management but is not legal advice or a jurisdiction-specific compliance determination.
OWASP ASVS 5.0.0 provides versioned application-security verification criteria whose scope and level require system context and accountable ownership.
WCAG 2.2 provides testable web accessibility success criteria, while conformance alone does not prove complete usability or accessibility for every user and context.
Versioned AI risk and community security taxonomies can prompt discovery but do not replace a system-specific threat model or confer certification.
The asset-to-threat-to-risk-to-control-to-evidence chain in this chapter is an original synthesis tool, not a formal external standard.
A policy or framework label is not control evidence until the deployment connects an objective to an implementation, verification method, evidence, owner, and disposition.
Logging for auditability should remain purpose-bound and minimized because excessive event content can create additional privacy and security exposure.
An FDE can prepare evidence and route a decision but cannot self-designate formal authority to accept legal, security, privacy, safety, audit, accessibility, or business risk.
Security, reliability, usability, accessibility, privacy, and other quality concerns interact but are not interchangeable and require contextual tradeoffs and evidence.
Production quality spans interacting functional, operational, security, reliability, performance, cost, usability, maintainability, and recovery concerns rather than happy-path correctness alone.
The vertical-slice coverage test, repository map, review lens, and debt record in this chapter are original FDE synthesis tools rather than formal standards.
Versioned OpenAPI, AsyncAPI, and JSON Schema artifacts can make interface structures testable but do not establish domain semantics, workflow correctness, or production behavior by themselves.
HTTP method semantics alone do not make an application operation safely retryable when intent equivalence or external completion is ambiguous.
Secure development and application verification should be integrated into implementation and review rather than added after a functional slice is complete.
A model is one replaceable component inside a production path whose contracts, data, policy, authorization, audit, operation, and failure behavior remain system responsibilities.
Release automation and consistency can reduce manual variance but do not replace review, verification, evidence, or recovery design.
A deterministic test double proves only the behavior encoded in that double and cannot establish the real dependency's semantics, authorization, performance, availability, or failure distribution.
A feature control reduces exposure only when default state, scope, owner, observability, interaction testing, expiry, and removal are explicit.
A clean, documented, automated local path improves reproducibility while remaining distinct from evidence in a representative customer environment.
Explicit debt records preserve the reason, consequence, owner, trigger, and exit condition of a compromise; an unowned TODO does not.
The cheapest-credible-evidence rule and risk-to-criterion-to-method-to-observation-to-limitation-to-disposition matrix are original FDE synthesis tools rather than formal standards.
Interface specifications and schemas can anchor structural contract tests while workflow semantics, authorization, data quality, and safe retry need additional assertions.
Passing a finite test or evaluation suite samples defined behavior under recorded conditions and does not prove the absence of security, safety, reliability, accessibility, or quality failures.
AI evaluation benefits from explicit tasks, cases or trials, data provenance, graders, traces or outcomes, a versioned harness, a suite, and a decision purpose.
Capability evaluation asks whether an approach can meet a task under defined conditions, while regression evaluation checks whether a changed system preserves accepted behavior.
An aggregate pass rate can conceal an unacceptable failure in a high-consequence workflow, user, equipment, region, or evidence-quality segment.
Evaluation data needs recorded provenance, permission, construction, version, split, leakage status, segment, correction history, and known representativeness limits.
Human, deterministic, and model-based graders require explicit rubrics and appropriate calibration; model graders can share failure modes and are not objective by assumption.
Deployment-like simulation can reveal behavior missed by static evaluation while still leaving production-tail, real-user, and real-dependency limitations.
Production monitoring of data, workflow, and model quality complements pre-release verification and cannot be replaced by service availability alone.
Versioned security, accessibility, software-quality, and layered AI-safety criteria can support release evidence without proving complete safety, security, accessibility, quality, or compliance.

User acceptance testing should observe representative users completing defined tasks with acceptance criteria; it is not an informal demonstration or transfer of formal risk authority to participants.
Deterministic assertions, statistical estimates, expert judgments, and user-acceptance observations support different claim types and should not be merged into an undifferentiated pass label.
Known limitations, failed criteria, and waivers require explicit consequence, owner, authority, scope, conditions, expiry, and release disposition.
The promise-to-failure-to-signal map, signal catalog, and diagnostic evidence tree are original FDE synthesis tools rather than formal standards.
Service indicators and objectives are most useful when they reflect user-relevant behavior and connect to a precommitted operational decision or tradeoff.
Metrics, traces, and logs provide distinct but correlatable telemetry signals, while current instrumentation APIs and product support remain version-sensitive.
Service availability alone cannot establish workflow usefulness, data quality, model quality, policy correctness, user adoption, or supportability.
Global averages can conceal degradation in a consequential cohort, site, region, workflow state, evidence-quality segment, or latency tail.
Production AI operation requires monitoring system, data, workflow, model, policy, review, fallback, and outcome behavior rather than model-service uptime alone.
Support demand and feedback are operating signals that can reveal service defects, exclusion, training burden, and adoption friction.
Telemetry should be purpose-bound, minimized, access-controlled, retained deliberately, and cost/cardinality constrained rather than collecting sensitive payloads by default.
Incident response should connect preparation, detection, response, recovery, and improvement to organizational cybersecurity risk management.
Data-quality and software-quality models can structure operational questions without prescribing local indicators or thresholds.
An alert without an accountable owner, urgency, evidence link, and first diagnostic action is notification noise rather than an operational control.
A dashboard is a view over selected evidence and does not by itself provide operability, diagnosis, response authority, or recovery capability.
